headline: Highest risk is data leakage and cascading error: Kestra can write/read shared files and egress broadly while Superset can consume upstream outputs, creating default-path exposure and trust-chain failures.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Kestra can read/write filesystem and emit messages/notifications; Superset consumes data via its API and analytics workflows, so a shared file or message bridge could carry attacker-controlled instructions. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than proven. Uncertainty pushes above low because both agents have broad I/O surfaces.
conditions: IF Kestra writes content that Superset later parses as instructions or SQL
IF both agents share a filesystem, queue, or copied artifact path
mitigations: Separate workspaces and mount points for the two agents
Disable automatic parsing of files/messages as instructions
Add provenance tags to all handoffs
Require manual review before Superset consumes Kestra outputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: Kestra touches logs, inputs, artifacts, database data, cloud storage data, messages, and notifications, and has broad network egress; Superset has allowlisted egress and can receive data through its API. If they share a workspace or hand off artifacts, sensitive data can flow from Kestra into Superset outputs or outbound requests. The pairwise leak path is plausible but not directly documented.
conditions: IF Kestra stores sensitive artifacts in a shared path readable by Superset
IF Superset exports or forwards data received from Kestra to its API or external destinations
mitigations: Keep sensitive artifacts out of shared directories
Restrict Kestra outputs to redacted summaries
Limit Superset datasets to non-sensitive sources
Review outbound destinations on both agents
Rotate or segregate credentials used by each agent

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Kestra has write_filesystem, execute_shell, spawn_subprocesses, and elevated root/docker.sock requests; Superset has network egress and API access. If both operate on the same host or directory, concurrent writes and state changes can collide, and Kestra's elevated privileges make the blast radius larger. The profiles do not show locking or isolation between them, so default safety is not established.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or database without locks
IF Kestra runs with root or docker.sock access on the same machine as Superset
mitigations: Run the agents in separate containers or VMs
Use distinct writable directories and databases
Disable root and docker.sock unless required
Add file-locking or transactional coordination
Stagger jobs so only one agent mutates shared state at a time

D_cascading_error.rationale: Kestra produces workflow definitions, logs, inputs, variables, artifacts, and notifications; Superset can consume upstream data through its API and present it as analytics. That creates a plausible chain where Kestra output becomes Superset input with limited verification. Superset is not documented as blindly trusting Kestra, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF Superset ingests Kestra-generated artifacts or metrics without validation
IF Kestra notifications are treated as authoritative facts in Superset dashboards
mitigations: Insert schema validation between agents
Mark Kestra outputs as untrusted until checked
Require human approval for downstream actions
Compare outputs against source-of-truth systems
Log and alert on malformed handoff records

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch shown. Kestra touches logs, messages, and cloud data, while Superset lists no sensitive data classes or special compliance constraints. Because no concrete mismatch is documented, only a low residual compliance risk is supportable.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through Kestra into Superset without a documented policy
IF retention or deletion settings differ between the two deployments
mitigations: Document data-class handling for both deployments
Align retention and deletion settings
Avoid routing regulated data through the pair
Review residency and access controls before production use
